ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: As this is a meta-analysis of published studies, no new ethical approval or consent was required.

We exploratorily also considered affiliation with A. Geraci, who has also emerged as a prolific contributor to this field. (h) Moreover, we assess the geographical generalizability of the effect by examining study location, coded by continent (North America, South America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania). (i) Finally, we exploratorily test whether preregistration status (preregistered vs. not preregistered) moderates the effect, as preregistered studies may yield more reliable estimates.
We also sought unpublished data by issuing calls on relevant online listservs (i.e., COGDEVSOC, DEVEUROPE, ICIS-listserv) and by directly contacting the most prolific authors in the field.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Margoni & Surian's (2018) meta-analysis update
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: After the failed attempt to replicate the Hamlin's hill paradigm's results (Lucca et al., 2025, Developmental Science), we plan to update the original meta-analysis published by Margoni and Surian in 2018 (Developmental Psychology) estimating the extent to which infants and toddlers (4-32 months) show a preference for prosocial/good agents over antisocial/bad agents. We will run a new meta-analysis which will also include all the data collected after the 2018's meta-analysis, both manual choice and preferential looking data, and published and unpublished experiments.
table.design_dependent_variables: The key dependent variable is the child's preference for either the prosocial/good agent or the antisocial/bad agent. In the experiments included in the meta-analysis, infants and toddlers are first presented with scenarios involving a prosocial agent (who can be a helper, a fair distributor, a giver, a comforter, etc.) and an antisocial agent (who can be a hinderer, an unfair distributor, a taker, a harmer, etc.). Next, participants are tested by being encouraged to reach for one of the agents (or toy offered by them) or to help (or give a treat to or share with) one of the agents. Alternatively, participants are presented with the two agents, and a looking preference is established by measuring to which agent participants look the longest. In this second case, two strategies are possible: first, we can consider the difference between the looking time spent on the prosocial vs. the antisocial agent (and convert it to Cohen's d, to analyze this data together with the difference between the proportion of infants who chose the prosocial agent in the manual reaching studies and chance level set at 50%); second, a count can be performed to calculate the number of infants who looked longer at the prosocial agent (in which case this data can be analyzed more straightforwardly, together with the proportion of infants who chose the prosocial agent in the manual reaching studies).
table.study_design_overview: In the meta-analysis, only experimental or social conditions will be included, i.e., conditions where a clearly prosocial agent is pitted against a clearly antisocial agent. All the other conditions in the papers we retrieve will be excluded.
table.statistical_tests:
We will first calculate an average-point estimate of the effect size from the retrieved studies, and its 95% confidence interval. We will conduct both fixed-effects and random-effects meta-analyses. Second, we will estimate heterogeneity and test for possible moderators. Among the moderators we will test for, the main ones will be: 

-age (inserted as a continuous predictor, in days, in a first analysis, and creating two groups of infants, those with age < 12,29 months and those with age > 12,29 months; to test whether the preference for prosocial agents increases with age)

-sample size (to test whether effect size decreases as sample size increases)

-the fact that the study is published or not (to test whether published studies overall report bigger effect sizes)

-the fact that the study is reported by the same lab (Hamlin's lab) that published the first original study that spearheaded much of the meta-analyzed research (to test whether independent labs report smaller effect sizes); here, we might also decide to include research published by former students of K. Hamlin in the Hamlin's lab category.

-the type of scenario (with 4 levels: help/hinder, fair/unfair, give/ take, other; to test whether we replicate the finding of the first meta-analysis for which give/take scenario was associated with the highest proportion of infants preferring the prosocial agent)

-the modality of stimulus presentation (with 2 levels: real vs. cartoon; or, in a second analysis: live show vs. movie; to test whether presenting infants with real characters or live shows facilitates the expression of a preference for prosociality)

-the type of DV (with 3 levels: reach, help, preferential looking; to test whether preferential looking experiments report bigger effects than manual reaching experiments; we might also run the same analysis with only 2 levels to more directly compare preferential looking to manual reaching studies)

-the type of agents shown to infants (with 3 levels: experimenters, puppets, simple geometrical shapes; to test whether interacting with real people facilitates the expression of a preference for prosociality)

Last, we will test for evidence of publication bias.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Outliers and participants excluded from the analyses in the studies we retrieve will also be excluded in the current meta-analysis. We will include experiments assessing infants' and toddlers' choices for prosociality vs. antisociality both with a manual reaching (or helping/offering) paradigm and a preferential looking paradigm. We will include infants between the youngest age we can find in the retrieved studies and 36 months of age.
table.sample_size: We will include all the relevant published and unpublished evidence we can retrieve.

report:

table.formatted: A significant Q-test confirmed the presence of heterogeneity, Q(181) = 627.92, p < .001.
table.expanded: A significant Q-test confirmed the presence of heterogeneity, Q(181) = 627.92, p < .001.
No significant moderation was observed, Q M (1) = 0.86, p = .353.
We found evidence of publication bias, with the intercept estimated as -0.31 [-0.59, -0.03], p = .032.
In this case, we did not find evidence of publication bias, with the slope estimated as 1.22 [-1.08, 3.51], p = .299.

table.formatted: As seen in Figure <ref type="figure">4A</ref>, age did not significantly moderate the effect size, Q M (1) = 0.46, p = .500, with the estimated effect of one additional month of age being ∆g = 0.12 [-0.23, 0.47].

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 105 columns across 5 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Of 5 scripts: 2 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. info.title: Infants' Social Evaluations Revisited: An Updated Meta-Analysis

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								University of Stavanger
								
									Norway

Department of Psychology
								Stanford University
								
									USA

text.text: As this is a meta-analysis of published studies, no new ethical approval or consent was required.
• Conducted during a replication crisis, this meta-analysis updates prior work, synthesizing 182 effect sizes from 4,089 infants.
• Infants show a consistent preference for prosocial over antisocial agents, with a metaanalytic proportion of 0.65.
• Preference for prosocial agents is robust across age, measure type, stimulus format and scenario, but moderated by sample size.
• No clear evidence of publication bias was detected.

Over the past two decades, a substantial number of studies have examined infants' and toddlers' responses to prosocial agents, who help, comfort, or act fairly, versus antisocial agents, who hinder, harm, or act unfairly.

This line of research was spearheaded by Hamlin et al. (2007), who presented 6-and 10-month-old preverbal infants with a scenario in which a central character, a wooden circle with large googly eyes, attempted to climb a hill.
text.formatted: This line of research was spearheaded by <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hamlin et al. (2007)</ref>, who presented 6-and 10-month-old preverbal infants with a scenario in which a central character, a wooden circle with large googly eyes, attempted to climb a hill.

text.text: Infants were then introduced to a prosocial agent, who assisted the climber, and an antisocial agent, who obstructed it.
When choosing between agents, most of the infants selected the prosocial helper rather than the antisocial hinderer.

This initial evidence was followed by numerous studies that extended the finding from a helper-hinderer distinction within the "hill" paradigm (e.g., Hamlin, 2013; Hamlin et al., 2010) to a broader preference for prosocial, morally good agents over antisocial, morally bad ones.
text.formatted: This initial evidence was followed by numerous studies that extended the finding from a helper-hinderer distinction within the "hill" paradigm (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Hamlin, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Hamlin et al., 2010)</ref> to a broader preference for prosocial, morally good agents over antisocial, morally bad ones.

text.text: Research has documented early-emerging preferences for agents who return resources rather than take them (e.g., Dahl et al., 2013; Hamlin and Wynn, 2011; Scola et al., 2015), distribute resources fairly rather than unfairly (e.g., Burns and Sommerville, 2014; Geraci and Surian, 2011; Lucca et al., 2018), and comfort or protect others from aggression rather than harm or ignore them (e.g., Biro, 2023; Buon et al., 2014; Kanakogi et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Research has documented early-emerging preferences for agents who return resources rather than take them (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Dahl et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Hamlin and Wynn, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Scola et al., 2015)</ref>, distribute resources fairly rather than unfairly (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Burns and Sommerville, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Geraci and Surian, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Lucca et al., 2018)</ref>, and comfort or protect others from aggression rather than harm or ignore them (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Biro, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Buon et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kanakogi et al., 2017</ref>).

text.text: An early-emerging capacity to distinguish and prefer prosocial over antisocial agentsthe focus of the present meta-analysis-is regarded as a key piece of evidence in debates on whether the foundations of human morality are built-in and present before the second birthday, equipping infants to navigate their social world, or whether they emerge only through extensive socialization and, potentially, language development beyond infancy (Hamlin, 2015b; Laurence and Margolis, 2024; Thomsen and Carey, 2013).
text.formatted: An early-emerging capacity to distinguish and prefer prosocial over antisocial agentsthe focus of the present meta-analysis-is regarded as a key piece of evidence in debates on whether the foundations of human morality are built-in and present before the second birthday, equipping infants to navigate their social world, or whether they emerge only through extensive socialization and, potentially, language development beyond infancy <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hamlin, 2015b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Laurence and Margolis, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Thomsen and Carey, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Contributing to the debate are also studies that examine infants' and toddlers' expectations about others' behavior.

This research shows that children under two years of age are sensitive to violations of several foundational moral principles (Baillargeon et al., 2026; Ting et al., 2020), including harm avoidance (Ting and Baillargeon, 2021), fairness-both distributive (e.g., Meristo and Surian, 2013; Sloane et al., 2012) and procedural (Surian and Margoni, 2020)-as well as ingroup support (e.g., Jin and Baillargeon, 2017; Pun et al., 2021), authority, which defines moral obligations for leaders and subordinates (Margoni and Thomsen, 2024; Margoni et al., 2018; Stavans and Baillargeon, 2019), and reciprocity (Jin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This research shows that children under two years of age are sensitive to violations of several foundational moral principles <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baillargeon et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Ting et al., 2020)</ref>, including harm avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Ting and Baillargeon, 2021)</ref>, fairness-both distributive (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Meristo and Surian, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Sloane et al., 2012)</ref> and procedural <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Surian and Margoni, 2020</ref>)-as well as ingroup support (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Jin and Baillargeon, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Pun et al., 2021)</ref>, authority, which defines moral obligations for leaders and subordinates <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Margoni and Thomsen, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Margoni et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Stavans and Baillargeon, 2019)</ref>, and reciprocity <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, the present metaanalysis is restricted to studies examining whether infants and toddlers exhibit a preference for prosocial over antisocial agents-that is, whether they display early-emerging, intuitive evaluations that may serve as precursors and continue to underlie adult moral judgments.
Critically, accumulating evidence of replication failures-including a notable multi-lab attempt-challenges claims of robust early-emerging preferences for prosociality.

To start, two studies attempting to replicate the seminal findings by Hamlin and colleagues failed to reproduce the effect: Salvadori et al. (2015) did not replicate Hamlin and Wynn (2011)'s results, and Schlingloff et al. (2020) reported similar null findings when revisiting Hamlin et al. (2007).

(2015)</ref> did not replicate <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Hamlin and Wynn (2011)</ref>'s results, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Schlingloff et al. (2020)</ref> reported similar null findings when revisiting <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hamlin et al. (2007)</ref>.

text.text: A number of studies have also failed to detect a reliable preference for prosociality across different paradigms and scenarios (Cowell and Decety, 2015; Holvoet et al., 2018 Holvoet et al., , 2019;; Licht et al., 2023; Nava et al., 2019; Scarf et al., 2012; Surian and Margoni, 2020; Tan and Hamlin, 2022, 2024; Vaporova and Zmyj, 2020; Wu et al., 2025).

text.text: Unpublished work further contributes to this picture, with several reports of null findings or failed replications (e.g., Abramson et al., 2016; Hamlin, 2016 Hamlin, , 2025;; Woo and Hamlin, 2016; Yuen and Hamlin, 2021).

text.text: Not all of these null findings, however, necessarily indicate genuine replication failures.

Some have been reinterpreted in light of methodological differences (Woo et al., 2025); for example, Scarf et al. (2012)'s results were later argued by Hamlin (2015a) to stem from variations in the stimuli used.

(2012)</ref>'s results were later argued by <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hamlin (2015a)</ref> to stem from variations in the stimuli used.

text.text: Others may simply reflect variability expected from sampling error, as discussed in Margoni and Shepperd (2020).

text.text: Nevertheless, concerns regarding the robustness of infants' preferences for prosociality remain well-founded.

This is exemplified by the recent ManyBabies large-scale, multi-lab collaboration (Lucca et al., 2025), which failed to reproduce the original effect reported by Hamlin et al. (2007), finding that only about 49% of infants (total N = 302 in the social condition) preferred the helper over the hinderer.

(2007)</ref>, finding that only about 49% of infants (total N = 302 in the social condition) preferred the helper over the hinderer.

text.text: This recent large-scale null result substantially reinforces existing concerns and signals that the field is experiencing a moment of crisis (Open Science Collaboration, 2015).
text.formatted: This recent large-scale null result substantially reinforces existing concerns and signals that the field is experiencing a moment of crisis <ref type="bibr">(Open Science Collaboration, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In this context, meta-analyzing the available data presents a timely opportunity to address unresolved questions.

Unlike most meta-analyses, which are typically conducted when enthusiasm in the field is high and a critical mass of positive findings has accumulatedconditions that are likely to inflate effect size estimates (ter Schure and Grünwald, 2019)-the present meta-analysis is conducted precisely amid growing uncertainty.
As such, it offers a chance to obtain a more realistic, less inflated estimate of the phenomenon of interest.

The present meta-analysis is a https://aspredicted.org/vjn6-73k3.pdf update and extension of the 2018 metaanalysis (Margoni and Surian, 2018), which synthesized published and unpublished studies retrieved up to 2017 and estimated a publication-bias-adjusted proportion of infants preferring prosocial over antisocial agents at 64% (95% CI [60, 69]).
text.formatted: The present meta-analysis is a <ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/vjn6-73k3.pdf">preregistered</ref> update and extension of the 2018 metaanalysis <ref type="bibr">(Margoni and Surian, 2018)</ref>, which synthesized published and unpublished studies retrieved up to 2017 and estimated a publication-bias-adjusted proportion of infants preferring prosocial over antisocial agents at 64% (95% CI <ref type="bibr">[60,</ref> <ref type="bibr">69]</ref>).

text.text: This new meta-analysis updates that estimate and examines potential moderators of heterogeneity across studies, with three main goals.

First, our main objective is to provide an updated estimate of the phenomenon of interest by not only incorporating published and unpublished evidence that appears after 2017, but also by including studies employing preferential looking paradigms alongside manual reaching tasks, which were the sole focus of the Margoni and Surian (2018)'s analysis.
Preferential looking studies were excluded from the original meta-analysis because only a limited number were available at the time, and their exclusion helped preserve methodological homogeneity.
Since then, however, the use of visual preference measures has grown substantially, partly reflecting the practical constraints on in-person testing imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic.
Because both manual and visual preferences are routinely interpreted as indexing sociomoral preferences in this literature, we included both approaches in the present meta-analysis.
This broader scope also allowed us to extend the age range to include infants younger than four months, who were previously excluded.

As in Margoni and Surian (2018), we test for publication bias and examine whether published studies report system-atically larger effects than unpublished ones, despite the growing ease of publishing null findings, particularly when studies are preregistered or involve direct replication attempts.
text.formatted: As in <ref type="bibr">Margoni and Surian (2018)</ref>, we test for publication bias and examine whether published studies report system-atically larger effects than unpublished ones, despite the growing ease of publishing null findings, particularly when studies are preregistered or involve direct replication attempts.

text.text: Second, in this meta-analysis, which uses a large dataset comprising about 4,000 participants, we examine whether the age of infants and toddlers (0-32 months, spanning the first 2.5 years of life) moderates their preference for prosocial agents.
This question is central because it allows us to evaluate competing theoretical accounts.
Finding age-related increases in prosocial choices would support the view that social experience and, possibly, early language development shape infants' sociomoral preferences.

In contrast, a rationalist account of the acquisition of prosocial preferences-while fully compatible with developmental change and the influence of social experience-would be particularly strengthened by the absence of significant age effects, together with evidence that infants and toddlers overall show a preference for prosociality.

In the present context, such a pattern would suggest that a propensity to prefer prosocial agents emerges very early in life, with limited social experience, and is potentially mediated by domain-specific learning mechanisms (Laurence and Margolis, 2024).
text.formatted: In the present context, such a pattern would suggest that a propensity to prefer prosocial agents emerges very early in life, with limited social experience, and is potentially mediated by domain-specific learning mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Laurence and Margolis, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, the presence or absence of developmental change provides a critical test of whether sociomoral preferences are shaped primarily through experience or reflect an early, stable predisposition, thereby further informing the debate between competing theories on the origins of human moral judgment.
Third, we examine several additional moderators to assess the generalizability and consistency of the effect.

These include (a) sample size, (b) scenario type (fair/unfair, help/hinder, give/take, other scenarios), (c) measure type (reach, help, visual preference), (d) stimulus format (live shows of real events, movies of real events, movies of cartoons), (e) type of agents presented (human confederates, puppets, shapes), (f) whether a prompt was used to elicit preferences, (g) laboratory affiliation (Hamlin and collaborators, Geraci and collaborators, independent labs), (h) study location, and (i) preregistration status.
(a) We begin with sample size, which is expected to influence the precision of the effect estimates.
Small samples can reduce estimate accuracy and are more susceptible to publication bias, potentially inflating estimates.
In contrast, large, well-powered tests provide more precise estimates.
Consequently, if the true effect is smaller than suggested by the full set of studies, we might expect an inverse relationship between the sample size and the strength of the observed effect.
More broadly, examining sample size helps evaluate the reliability and robustness of the overall meta-analytic estimate.
(b) Next, we test whether effect sizes vary across the main scenario types (fair/unfair, help/hinder, give/take, and other scenarios such as comforting/ignoring).

Notably, one of the key findings of Margoni and Surian (2018) was that the type of scenario moderated the preference of the infants and toddlers, with help/hinder scenarios yielding significantly weaker effects than give/take scenarios, by nearly 10 percentage points in the average estimate.
text.formatted: Notably, one of the key findings of <ref type="bibr">Margoni and Surian (2018)</ref> was that the type of scenario moderated the preference of the infants and toddlers, with help/hinder scenarios yielding significantly weaker effects than give/take scenarios, by nearly 10 percentage points in the average estimate.

text.text: We therefore test whether this pattern replicates in the present meta-analysis, which also incorporates the data from the large-scale multi-lab replication attempt by Lucca et al. (2025), a study that relied exclusively on a help/hinder paradigm and did not yield significant effects. (c) Additionally, we examine the impact of measure type, that is, whether infants' preferences were inferred from manual choices, helping decisions, or visual attention.
text.formatted: We therefore test whether this pattern replicates in the present meta-analysis, which also incorporates the data from the large-scale multi-lab replication attempt by <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lucca et al. (2025)</ref>, a study that relied exclusively on a help/hinder paradigm and did not yield significant effects. (c) Additionally, we examine the impact of measure type, that is, whether infants' preferences were inferred from manual choices, helping decisions, or visual attention.

text.text: Visual preference measures are a novel addition in this meta-analysis, not included in Margoni and Surian (2018).
text.formatted: Visual preference measures are a novel addition in this meta-analysis, not included in <ref type="bibr">Margoni and Surian (2018)</ref>.

text.text: We specifically explore whether visual measures confer an advantage over manual reaching measures, which were employed in most prior failed replications.
Three further factors relate to procedure design.
We test whether (d1) scenario delivery mode (movies vs. live shows) and (d2) scenario presentation format (cartoons vs. real events, irrespective of delivery mode) moderate the effect.
However, because no studies employed live cartoon shows, we coded a single (d) stimulus format moderator with three levels: live shows of real events, movies of real events, and movies of cartoons.

Infants may be predisposed to attend more to real-life social interactions, given that our evolutionary history primarily exposed us to three-dimensional, real-world agents rather than two-dimensional representations.
Consequently, live shows or videos of real events might facilitate better processing and understanding.
Conversely, cartoons could offer an advantage because their simplified, less perceptually complex stimuli may reduce cognitive demands and make the social interactions easier to follow.

While the Margoni and Surian (2018) analysis did not find evidence for an effect of these moderators, we revisit this question using a substantially larger dataset. (e) We also test whether the type of agents presented to infants (human confederates, puppets, or foam shapes) moderates the effect.
text.formatted: While the <ref type="bibr">Margoni and Surian (2018)</ref> analysis did not find evidence for an effect of these moderators, we revisit this question using a substantially larger dataset. (e) We also test whether the type of agents presented to infants (human confederates, puppets, or foam shapes) moderates the effect.

text.text: Based on the reasoning outlined above for the predictions regarding scenario delivery mode and presentation format, interactions involving human confederates might be expected to produce the strongest effects, followed by puppets and foam shapes. (f) Last, we test whether providing infants and toddlers with a prompt to express their preference facilitates task engagement and overall produces stronger effects compared to when no prompt is given.
Next, we investigate potential moderators related to study provenance and preregistration. (g) We test laboratory affiliation (Hamlin's group versus independent labs) as moderator.

Given that K. Hamlin initiated this research area and contributed a substantial portion of the data, which might also be affected by a winner's curse effect-i.e., the tendency for initial studies to systematically overestimate true effect sizes (Gelman and Loken, 2014)-and considering several failed replication attempts (reviewed above), we assess whether effect sizes are reliably smaller in studies conducted by independent labs.
text.formatted: Given that K. Hamlin initiated this research area and contributed a substantial portion of the data, which might also be affected by a winner's curse effect-i.e., the tendency for initial studies to systematically overestimate true effect sizes <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gelman and Loken, 2014</ref>)-and considering several failed replication attempts (reviewed above), we assess whether effect sizes are reliably smaller in studies conducted by independent labs.

text.text: We exploratorily also considered affiliation with A. Geraci, who has also emerged as a prolific contributor to this field. (h) Moreover, we assess the geographical generalizability of the effect by examining study location, coded by continent (North America, South America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania). (i) Finally, we exploratorily test whether preregistration status (preregistered vs. not preregistered) moderates the effect, as preregistered studies may yield more reliable estimates.

More broadly, evaluating the impact of all the methodological factors outlined above provides insight into the robustness and generalizability of infants' preferences for prosociality over antisociality.

The identification of relevant studies was undertaken (between spring and summer 2025) through a systematic search of PsycINFO, MEDLINE, and Google Scholar, conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines (see Figure ??
for the corresponding PRISMA flow diagram).
An abstract-level search was performed employing the keywords infant* or toddler* and moral*, help*, hinder*, harm*, fair*, comfort*, prosocial* or prefer*.
We thus conducted a search for relevant studies published up to 2025.

Studies from the original metaanalysis were directly incorporated, previously excluded studies were re-evaluated under the revised inclusion criteria, and additional eligible studies were identified through database searches.

Studies were included according to the following criteria: (a) The study evaluated infants' choices using a manual task (which could involve a manual choice paradigm, a selective helping paradigm, or a paradigm in which children were encouraged to provide goods to one of two characters) or a preferential looking task.
We did not include violation of expectation studies.

Namely, we included only studies that could reveal infants' sociomoral assessments or preferences (Choi and Luo, 2023), rather than their expectations (measured via the violation-of-expectation paradigm; Margoni et al., 2024). (b) Infants were presented with an opportunity to indicate a preference between a "morally good" and a "morally bad" character.
text.formatted: Namely, we included only studies that could reveal infants' sociomoral assessments or preferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Choi and Luo, 2023)</ref>, rather than their expectations (measured via the violation-of-expectation paradigm; <ref type="bibr">Margoni et al., 2024)</ref>. (b) Infants were presented with an opportunity to indicate a preference between a "morally good" and a "morally bad" character.

text.text: In this context, a morally good character could be depicted as a helping agent, a fair distributor, a giver, or an agent who provides comfort to others or intervenes in their defense when they are subjected to aggression.

Conversely, a morally bad character could be portrayed as a hindering agent, an unfair distributor, a keeper/taker, or an agent who disregards others in distress. (c) The sample consisted of infants and toddlers between 0 and 36 months of age.
Relative to the original 2018 meta-analysis, the present meta-analysis differs in two main aspects.
First, studies employing preferential looking paradigms have been included.
Second, the age range has been extended to cover the first four months of life, which were previously excluded.
Following the main search on the databases, we conducted a supplementary screening of the reference lists of the retrieved articles to identify any additional relevant published studies.
We also sought unpublished data by issuing calls on relevant online listservs (i.e., COGDEVSOC, DEVEUROPE, ICIS-listserv) and by directly contacting the most prolific authors in the field.

This search yielded a total of 65 studies (representing an increase of 39 studies compared to the original meta-analysis) encompassing k = 183 effect sizes (152 published, 31 unpublished), with an aggregate sample of 4,090 unique participants, 2,846 more than in the previous meta-analysis.

Note that two studies (k = 3 effect sizes) were initially identified as unpublished but were coded as published in the final analyses because they appeared in print before the analyses were finalized, and that one effect size was excluded because it was based on a single participant (n = 1), precluding the computation of a smallsample corrected effect size.
Thus, the final analytic dataset comprised k = 182 effect sizes.

A detailed list of the included studies is provided in the online Supplemental Material (SM) uploaded on https://osf.io/r4av3/?view_only=aa69cf6c08884058b0cc72a75d55347c and a visual summary is presented in the forest plot displayed in Figure 1.

text.text: Two coders (the study's authors) who were aware of the meta-analysis objectives, examined each article and independently coded its methodological attributes and reported outcomes.
Each evaluator also assessed whether the experiments satisfied the inclusion criteria.
Initial inter-rater agreement averaged 99% across all coded variables, with discrepancies subsequently resolved through discussion (approximately 30 discrepancies were resolved).
In line with the procedures of the original meta-analysis and the preregistration, we coded the following 13 variables.
(1) Published status: Coded as whether the study had been published.

(2) Age: We coded both the sample mean age (in days) and, consistent with the original meta-analysis, a binary classification of young versus old; the young category was defined as a mean age ≤ 12 months, 29 days.
(3) Sample size.

(4) Scenario type: Coded according to the type of event presented to infants or toddlers, including helping vs. hindering, fair vs. unfair (distributive) actions, giving/returning vs. taking objects, or other sociomoral interactions (e.g., harm/ignore vs. comfort) (for each scenario type, we included only cases in which agents with at least positive versus at least negative intentions were contrasted, excluding cases in which the outcomes contradicted the agent's intentions). ( 5) Measure type: We coded infants' responses into three categories: reach (if infants were prompted to reach for one of the agents or an object offered by them), help (if infants were encouraged to give a treat or share with one of the agents), or visual (if the preference was inferred from looking time within a preferential-looking study). ( 6) Scenario delivery mode: Coded as live show or movie (e.g., Hamlin et al. (2007)'s wooden hill version was coded as a live show). ( 7) Scenario presentation format: Coded as real events (live shows or staged movies with puppets or human actors) versus cartoons.

(13) Dependent Variable: Last, we recorded, for manual-reaching studies, the number of participants showing a manual preference for the prosocial agent; for preferential-looking studies, we coded whichever of the following were reported or available: average looking times toward the prosocial and antisocial agents, corresponding t-test values, and/or the percentage of time spent looking at the prosocial agent.

text.text: Before conducting the analyses, each outcome was converted into Cohen's d and its corresponding variance.
These values were computed following three steps, depending on what information was available in each experiment.

For studies with manual choice outcomes ("reach" or "help"), we converted the log odds ratio of choosing the prosocial agent to Cohen's π , and Var(d) = 1 p + 1 1-p , where p is the proportion of infants choosing the prosocial agent (Hasselblad and Hedges, 1995).
text.formatted: For studies with manual choice outcomes ("reach" or "help"), we converted the log odds ratio of choosing the prosocial agent to Cohen's π , and Var(d) = 1 p + 1 1-p , where p is the proportion of infants choosing the prosocial agent <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hasselblad and Hedges, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: For studies with looking time outcomes, we used t-statistics where available, with d = t √ n .
When unavailable, we used the mean and standard deviation for s, the proportion of looking time toward the prosocial agent, with (Borenstein, 2009).
text.formatted: When unavailable, we used the mean and standard deviation for s, the proportion of looking time toward the prosocial agent, with <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Borenstein, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: A few studies only reported the number of participants who looked more to the prosocial agent; in those cases, we used the same calculation as the binary manual choice outcomes.
Many of the included effect sizes had small sample sizes, for which d is a biased estimate; thus, we used Hedges' small-sample correction, transforming Cohen's d into Hedges' g (Hedges, 1981).
text.formatted: Many of the included effect sizes had small sample sizes, for which d is a biased estimate; thus, we used Hedges' small-sample correction, transforming Cohen's d into Hedges' g <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hedges, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: For interpretability, all figures (except Figure 2) present Hedges' g backtransformed into raw proportions (infants or toddlers expressing a preference for the prosocial agent divided by sample size).

text.text: To do so, the odds ratio was recovered as OR = exp g • π √ 3 , then converted to a proportion via p = OR 1+OR .
The same transformation was applied to the confidence interval bounds of g.

We begin by calculating an average point estimate of the effect size for infants' preference for prosocial over antisocial agents, reporting both Hedges' g and its back-transformation into raw proportions to improve interpretability.
The included studies contributed a total of k = 182 effect sizes to analyze (dataset available at https://osf.io/r4av3/?view_only=aa69cf6c08884058b0cc72a75d55347c).

text.text: We used a random-effects meta-analysis to account for heterogeneity across studies, with a nested random structure of participant group within paper.
We report all estimates with their 95% confidence intervals.
A forest plot is shown in Figure 1; note that the forest plot displays effect sizes aggregated by paper for concision, but all analyses treated each effect size separately.
text.formatted: A forest plot is shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>; note that the forest plot displays effect sizes aggregated by paper for concision, but all analyses treated each effect size separately.

text.text: The estimated meta-analytic effect size was g = 0.34 [0.26, 0.41].
When back-transformed to raw proportions, this effect size corresponds to 0.65 [0.61, 0.68].
A significant Q-test confirmed the presence of heterogeneity, Q(181) = 627.92, p < .001.
text.formatted: A significant Q-test confirmed the presence of heterogeneity, Q(181) = 627.92, p < .001.

text.text: The estimated variance across papers was σ2 = 0.04, and the estimated variance across participant groups within papers was σ2 = 0.07.
Given this variability between studies, we proceeded to examine potential moderators to identify factors that might account for differences in infants' preferences across experiments.

We fit two hierarchical meta-regression models.

The first was a main-effects model that included all moderators simultaneously as fixed effects, thus estimating the association of each moderator with effect size while adjusting for the remaining moderators.
The second was an interaction model containing theoretically motivated interaction terms among selected moderators.
Both models included random intercepts of participant group nested within study.
Post-hoc pairwise contrasts were evaluated using Tukey's HSD correction.
In the following sections, we first present the results of the main-effects model, followed by the interaction model.

It is possible that the moderators had effects that were non-independent.
Thus, we considered three possible sets of interaction effects in an extended model.
First, the response measure used may have depended on the stimulus format and the scenario (e.g., preferential looking is more common with movies than with live shows).
Second, the scenarios used may differ depending on the laboratory affiliation, as some laboratories may prefer research questions related to particular scenarios.

Third, the age of the children may have affected the choices of scenario, measure, and stimulus format (e.g., looking time measures tend to be used with younger infants who are less able to reliably reach).

The present preregistered meta-analysis provides an updated estimate of infants' and toddlers' preference for prosociality over antisociality.

This analysis refines the estimate originally reported by Margoni and Surian (2018) and was undertaken amid a replication crisis, particularly following the large-scale failed replication by the ManyBabies collabo-ration (Lucca et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This analysis refines the estimate originally reported by <ref type="bibr">Margoni and Surian (2018)</ref> and was undertaken amid a replication crisis, particularly following the large-scale failed replication by the ManyBabies collabo-ration <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lucca et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Across 182 effect sizes, we estimated that 65% [61%, 68%] of infants and toddlers (0-32 months) preferred a prosocial agent, corresponding to a Hedges' g = 0.34 [0.26, 0.41].
No clear evidence for publication bias was detected.
Notably, the estimated proportion remained virtually identical to the publication-bias-adjusted estimate reported in the previous meta-analysis, which was 64% [60%, 69%].
We will return later to the interpretation of what a proportion of 0.65 may signify.
For now, we note that, compared to the previous meta-analysis, the present one incorporated 121 new independent effect sizes and 2,845 additional participants.

Importantly, these additions comprised numerous positive findings alongside the several failed replications reported in recent years, while also broadening the evidence base to include visual-preference paradigms.

Yet, because measure type (preferential-looking vs. manual-reaching) did not moderate the magnitude of the effect, the remarkable stability of the updated estimate appears to be driven primarily by the coexistence of both successful and unsuccessful replications, rather than by the inclusion of a wider range of methodological approaches.

Whereas we found no clear evidence of publication bias, no indication that published studies reported larger effects than unpublished ones, and no indication that preregistration status moderated the effect size, the present meta-analysis revealed a possible effect of sample size.
Specifically, when including outliers (i.e., four effect sizes associated with n ∈ [171, 442]), experiments with larger samples yielded smaller effects.
This finding might temper the apparent stability of the updated estimate relative to the prior meta-analysis.

Because larger samples provide more precise estimates, the observation that greater precision is associated with smaller effects raises the possibility that the current estimate may still be inflated relative to the true population parameter.

However, this association between sample size and effect size was attenuated and no longer reached conventional levels of statistical significance after excluding outliers (p = .088), while retaining the same negative direction.
Consequently, additional large-scale investigations will be needed to determine whether this pattern is robust.
A central finding of the current meta-analysis is that age (5-981 days) did not moderate infants' and toddlers' preference for prosocial agents.

This result suggests that general developmental changes during the first two years of life, as well as the social input infants receive during this period-central to empiricist accounts of social preference development-do not substantially influence infant sociomoral preferences.

The absence of age effects, together with the observation that a significant proportion of both younger and older infants show a preference for prosocial over antisocial agents, indicates that a propensity to favor prosociality emerges early and with limited social experience, consistent with rationalist accounts of social development (Laurence & Margolis, 2024).

text.text: In other words, sociomoral preferences may be acquired through domain-specific learning mechanisms and reflect stable, potentially biologically prepared tendencies (Cosmides & Tooby, 1992).
text.formatted: In other words, sociomoral preferences may be acquired through domain-specific learning mechanisms and reflect stable, potentially biologically prepared tendencies <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cosmides & Tooby, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, we found no evidence of cross-cultural variability: study location (North America, Europe, Asia, Oceania) did not moderate the effect size, which may further support rationalist accounts.
More broadly, these data offer a concrete empirical benchmark for theories of the origins and early development of human moral cognition.
We also found no clear evidence that scenario type (fair/unfair, give/take, help/hinder, other) moderated the effect size.

Although help/hinder scenarios yielded a descriptively lower average estimate (0.62) than other types-particularly give/take and other scenarios (0.70 and 0.74 respectively)-no pairwise contrasts survived Tukey's HSD correction.
Consequently, the significant effect-size difference between give/take and help/hinder scenarios reported in the 2018 meta-analysis was not fully replicated.

This null result is notable, as reproducing that difference could have offered a partial explanation for the nonsignificant findings of the recent ManyBabies replication (Lucca et al., 2025), which used a help/hinder paradigm.
text.formatted: This null result is notable, as reproducing that difference could have offered a partial explanation for the nonsignificant findings of the recent ManyBabies replication <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Lucca et al., 2025)</ref>, which used a help/hinder paradigm.

text.text: Another null finding concerned measure type.

Unlike the previous meta-analysis, the current analysis included not only studies using manual reaching or selective helping measures, but also experiments assessing visual preference to test whether preferential-looking paradigms yield larger effects than manual-reaching measures.

No such effect was observed, indicating that effect sizes were consistent across measurement types-a pattern broadly consistent with evidence that looking and choosing often reflect related underlying processes (Hagihara et al., 2021; Hendrickson et al., 2015).
text.formatted: No such effect was observed, indicating that effect sizes were consistent across measurement types-a pattern broadly consistent with evidence that looking and choosing often reflect related underlying processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hagihara et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hendrickson et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Several other potential moderators yielded null effects, highlighting the consistency of the effect size across these factors.
First, we examined whether the presentation format of the stimuli (live shows of real events, movies of real events, or cartoon movies) moderated the effect size.

One possibility is that live presentations yield stronger effects than video-based presentations because infants may be especially attuned to real-life social interactions, reflecting an evolutionary history dominated by three-dimensional and real-world agents.
Relatedly, the video deficit effect suggests that young children often learn less from video than from comparable live presentations (Strouse & Samson, 2021).
text.formatted: Relatedly, the video deficit effect suggests that young children often learn less from video than from comparable live presentations <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Strouse & Samson, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Live interactions may therefore facilitate more effective processing and understanding of social behavior.

In addition, movie-based tasks (as in the recent failed replication by Lucca et al., 2025) may require infants to establish a correspondence between agents previously seen on screen and those subsequently encountered in the live test phase, and, more broadly, agents introduced in live shows may be experienced as more immediate and socially meaningful interaction partners than agents introduced via video, thus facilitating the effect.
text.formatted: In addition, movie-based tasks (as in the recent failed replication by <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lucca et al., 2025)</ref> may require infants to establish a correspondence between agents previously seen on screen and those subsequently encountered in the live test phase, and, more broadly, agents introduced in live shows may be experienced as more immediate and socially meaningful interaction partners than agents introduced via video, thus facilitating the effect.

text.text: Consistent with these possibilities, live shows were descriptively associated with stronger effects (0.69) than either type of movie presentation (0.63 and 0.60 for real events and cartoons, respectively).
However, stimulus format did not significantly moderate the effect size, indicating that these differences were only descriptive.
Consequently, any interpretation of this pattern remains speculative.

Second, two potential procedural moderators were examined: the type of agents used to assess infants' preferences (experimenter, puppet, or geometric-shape agents) and type of prompt employed (question "Who do you like?", no prompt, or other instructions).
Neither moderated the effect size, a pattern consistent with the previous meta-analysis.

Third, contrary to the previous meta-analysis, which reported an effect of laboratory affiliationspecifically that K. Hamlin's group produced larger effect sizes than independent laboratories when considering help/hinder and give/take effect sizes-the current meta-analysis found no such evidence.

However, an exploratory analysis based on the concept of "research allegiance" (Munder et al., 2013), which classified effects reported by B. Woo, a former student of K. Hamlin who may employ similar experimental protocols and methodological practices, as part of Hamlin's group, instead suggested larger effects in Hamlin-affiliated laboratories, with approximately 70% of children preferring the prosocial agent compared to 61% in independent laboratories.

text.text: By contrast, an exploratory analysis of Geraci laboratory affiliation, motivated by Geraci's emergence as the second most prolific contributor to this literature after Hamlin, revealed a significant moderating effect, with studies from the Geraci lab yielding larger effect sizes (75%) than studies from other laboratories (63%).

Given that much of the evidence on infants' preferences for fair versus unfair agents specifically originates from this laboratory, this finding highlights the importance of additional independent replications to establish the robustness and generalizability of the effect across research groups.
We estimated that 65% of infants and toddlers preferred prosocial over antisocial agents.
How should this figure be interpreted?

To begin, this proportion does not fall below the publication-bias-adjusted estimate reported in the previous meta-analysis, yet it is markedly lower than the original effect size reported by Hamlin et al. (2007), where all 6-month-old infants and the vast majority (88%) of 10-month-olds preferred the prosocial agent.

text.text: At the same time, our meta-analytic estimate diverges substantially from several failed replications, most notably Lucca et al. (2025).
text.formatted: At the same time, our meta-analytic estimate diverges substantially from several failed replications, most notably <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lucca et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: It is worth considering some potential reasons for the surprising deviation in results between the present meta-analysis and their multi-lab replication.
First, Lucca et al. ( 2025) used a single methodological paradigm-the hill helping/hindering paradigm using shape agents displayed via video.
text.formatted: First, Lucca et al. ( <ref type="formula">2025</ref>) used a single methodological paradigm-the hill helping/hindering paradigm using shape agents displayed via video.

text.text: Thus, the failed replication represents one specific set of stimuli under one methodological procedure, and it is possible that the observed null results may not generalize to other stimuli and procedures.

Second, the substantial between-lab heterogeneity observed in Lucca et al. (2025) suggests that there may be other population-or lab-related variance that remained to be explained despite their unified stimuli and procedure (e.g., variation in how labs "warmed up" with infants); as such information was not captured by the multi-lab replication (nor, indeed, by most of the studies in our meta-analysis), it is difficult to predict how such variation may affect the generalizability of the findings.
text.formatted: Second, the substantial between-lab heterogeneity observed in <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lucca et al. (2025)</ref> suggests that there may be other population-or lab-related variance that remained to be explained despite their unified stimuli and procedure (e.g., variation in how labs "warmed up" with infants); as such information was not captured by the multi-lab replication (nor, indeed, by most of the studies in our meta-analysis), it is difficult to predict how such variation may affect the generalizability of the findings.

text.text: Third, the discrepancy between our meta-analytic estimate and the null finding in Lucca et al. (2025) could be considered in light of a broader methodological pattern in psychology. Kvarven et al. (2020) compared 15 psychological phenomena for which both a meta-analysis and a large preregistered multi-laboratory replication were available and found that meta-analytic effect sizes were significantly larger than replication effect sizes in 12 of the 15 cases, with meta-analytic estimates being, on average, nearly three times as large.

(2025)</ref> could be considered in light of a broader methodological pattern in psychology. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kvarven et al. (2020)</ref> compared 15 psychological phenomena for which both a meta-analysis and a large preregistered multi-laboratory replication were available and found that meta-analytic effect sizes were significantly larger than replication effect sizes in 12 of the 15 cases, with meta-analytic estimates being, on average, nearly three times as large.

text.text: Thus, divergence between meta-analytic and replication-based estimates is not unusual.
At the same time, neither approach can be assumed to provide a uniquely accurate estimate of the underlying effect.

Large-scale replications minimize concerns about publication bias and selective reporting but typically examine a single operationalization under highly standardized conditions, whereas meta-analyses aggregate evidence across a broader range of populations, stimuli, and procedures while remaining vulnerable to biases and heterogeneity in the underlying literature.

Consequently, differences between the present meta-analysis and Lucca et al. (2025) may reflect not only discrepancies in effect-size estimation but also differences in the scope of the phenomena being captured.
text.formatted: Consequently, differences between the present meta-analysis and <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lucca et al. (2025)</ref> may reflect not only discrepancies in effect-size estimation but also differences in the scope of the phenomena being captured.

text.text: Taken together, these observations suggest that it would be premature to dismiss evidence for an early-emerging preference for prosociality.
Such a conclusion would rely primarily on null results from individual experiments, while neglecting the aggregate evidence synthesized here.
Pooling all available data reveals that slightly more than three out of five infants prefer prosocial over antisocial agents.
Interpreting this point estimate requires considering what manual choice or visual attention measures actually capture.
This is not a trivial task.

However, we believe that one of the most informative aspects of these tests is that-together with converging evidence from violation-of-expectation studies (e.g., Jin and Baillargeon, 2017; Margoni et al., 2018; Sloane et al., 2012; Ting and Baillargeon, 2021)-they suggest that infants possess a rudimentary moral sensitivity that enables them to distinguish between morally positive and negative actions.
text.formatted: However, we believe that one of the most informative aspects of these tests is that-together with converging evidence from violation-of-expectation studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Jin and Baillargeon, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Margoni et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Sloane et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Ting and Baillargeon, 2021)</ref>-they suggest that infants possess a rudimentary moral sensitivity that enables them to distinguish between morally positive and negative actions.

text.text: Accordingly, rather than viewing these paradigms solely as tests of prosocial preference, they may first be understood as demonstrating that infants reliably distinguish between agents-evidenced by non-random choices or differential attention.
Building on this foundation, two further questions arise.
First, do these paradigms reveal a true preference rather than curiosity or avoidance?

Although manual reaching and looking-time measures are typically interpreted as indicators of preference, they might alternatively reflect general curiosity toward one agent or an adaptive tendency to approach agents perceived as less threatening or relatively more beneficial-interpretations that partly even depend on how "preference" is conceptually defined.
Second, to what extent does the estimated mean proportion of 0.65 conceal individual differences in infants' and toddlers' responses?
At present, the available data do not permit a definitive answer (although, see Tan et al., 2018).
text.formatted: At present, the available data do not permit a definitive answer (although, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Tan et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Future theoretical and empirical work is needed to investigate whether infants exhibit systematic individual differences in their attraction to prosocial versus antisocial agents, or in their relative curiosity toward these characters (see Nighbor et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Future theoretical and empirical work is needed to investigate whether infants exhibit systematic individual differences in their attraction to prosocial versus antisocial agents, or in their relative curiosity toward these characters (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Nighbor et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: And further work is needed to uncover the cognitive mechanisms that lead children to ostensibly prefer one of the two agents.
The current meta-analysis estimates that 65% of infants and toddlers (0-32 months) prefer prosocial over antisocial agents.
This estimate appears robust to publication bias and is generally consistent across a range of potential moderators.
Notably, it is not influenced by age or study location, findings that lend support to rationalist accounts of moral sense acquisition.
However, when including outliers, the effect size was moderated by sample size, with larger studies reporting smaller effects.
This pattern tempers enthusiasm for the estimate, which, despite numerous recent failed replications, remains largely consistent with the previous meta-analysis.
The present work extends that earlier synthesis and provides an updated perspective in the context of the ongoing replication crisis.
